faq.q: What is the best iPhone navigation app for motorcycle touring?
faq.a: For touring specifically, VisorUp is our top pick because it is built for the job. Its route builder lets you set a road preference (fast, curvy or twisty), plan multi-day trips with day breaks, and drop in automatic fuel stops from 9,913 UK stations. Live Ride Mode then gives turn-by-turn directions, speed and ETA, optional voice guidance and automatic rerouting. For general point-to-point navigation, Apple Maps and Google Maps are excellent free alternatives.

faq.q: Is Apple Maps good enough for motorcycle navigation?
faq.a: Yes, for straightforward navigation and finding services Apple Maps is very capable, and it integrates neatly with CarPlay and offline downloads. What it does not do is plan a deliberately scenic, twisty route or fuel stops the way a touring app does. Many riders use Apple Maps for getting to the start of a ride and a touring app such as VisorUp or Kurviger for the interesting part.

faq.q: Which iPhone app plans the curviest roads?
faq.a: Kurviger and Calimoto both specialise in twisty, motorway-avoiding routes, and VisorUp offers a curvy and a twisty road preference in its route builder. If your priority is squeezing every bend out of a day's ride, try Kurviger's routing and compare it with VisorUp's twisty preference to see which suits your area of the country.

faq.q: Do iPhone navigation apps work without signal?
faq.a: They can, but only if you prepare. VisorUp caches your route for offline use, and Apple Maps, Google Maps, Kurviger and OS Maps all support downloading map areas in advance. This is essential in rural Britain, where signal is unreliable. Download the entire region you plan to ride, not just the route line, so you are covered if you divert. See our guide to offline maps for motorcycle touring for the full process.

faq.q: Should I use my iPhone or buy a dedicated GPS?
faq.a: Both work well. A dedicated GPS such as a Garmin Zumo or TomTom Rider has a sunlight-readable, waterproof, glove-friendly screen and keeps your phone in your pocket, but costs £250-500. An iPhone is free to press into service, always has current maps and does far more. Our full comparison in GPS vs phone for motorcycle navigation weighs it up in detail.

content:
Choosing the Right iPhone Navigation App

There is no single best iPhone navigation app for motorcycling, because riders want different things. Some want the fastest way to a friend's house, some want the twistiest possible route across a national park, and some want Ordnance Survey detail for exploring green lanes and back roads. The good news is that iOS covers all of these, often for free. This guide compares the leading options for UK touring in 2026 and helps you pick the right tool for each job.

One point applies to every app here: an iPhone needs the right hardware to navigate reliably on a bike. Use a vibration-dampening mount to protect the camera, wire in a power supply to survive a full day, and fit a weatherproof case or screen for British rain. With that sorted, here is how the apps stack up.

VisorUp: Built for UK Touring

VisorUp is our recommended starting point because it is designed specifically for touring Britain rather than adapted from car navigation. The route builder uses drag-and-drop waypoints and a road-preference control, so you can ask for a fast, curvy or twisty route between the same two points. It plots automatic fuel stops roughly every 100 miles from 9,913 UK fuel stations, and it lets you add any of 1,889 curated points of interest to your route with a single tap.

Out on the road, Live Ride Mode provides GPS tracking, turn-by-turn navigation, a speed and ETA display, optional voice prompts and automatic rerouting if you go off course. You can plan multi-day tours with day breaks, cache routes for offline use, and export any route as a GPX file to share with your group. It is free and ad-free, which makes it an easy first install. For everything the app does beyond navigation, see our roundup of the best iOS apps for motorcycle riding.

Apple Maps

Apple Maps has become a genuinely strong navigator. It is fast, clean, integrates tightly with CarPlay and Siri, and supports offline downloads. For getting reliably from A to B, checking traffic and finding fuel or food, it is excellent and completely free. Its limitation for riders is that it optimises for efficiency, not enjoyment, so it will not deliberately route you along the best roads. Use it for transit stages and services, and switch to a touring app for the ride itself.

Google Maps

Google Maps remains the best app for finding things: opening hours, reviews, fuel stations, cafes and accommodation. Its business data is unmatched. As a pure navigator it behaves much like Apple Maps, prioritising speed over scenery. Download offline areas before rural riding, because Google Maps leans heavily on a data connection.

Kurviger and Calimoto

These two are the enthusiasts' choice for curvy-road routing. Kurviger actively hunts out bends and avoids motorways by default, with GPX import and export and offline routing in the premium tier (around £20 a year). Calimoto does something similar and adds a rider community sharing routes and ratings, with a glove-friendly riding interface (premium around £30 a year). Both pair well with VisorUp: plan the scenic core in one and manage fuel, POIs and logistics in the other.

OS Maps

OS Maps (around £24 a year) is the definitive UK mapping app. Ordnance Survey's 1:25,000 mapping shows every track, path, building and contour, and its offline downloads are superb. It is not a turn-by-turn navigator in the usual sense, but for exploring remote back roads, unclassified lanes and terrain it is unrivalled. Serious explorers keep it installed alongside a routing app.

Ride Recording: Scenic and Relive

If you like to log and relive your rides, Scenic is a well-regarded iOS motorcycle route recorder and planner, and Relive turns your GPS track into a shareable 3D flyover video. Neither is a primary navigator, but they are lovely for capturing a tour. We cover these more fully in our guide to the best iOS apps for trip planning and ride tracking.

Our Recommended iPhone Navigation Stack

For most UK riders, the winning combination is VisorUp for touring routes and live navigation, Apple Maps or Google Maps for services and transit, OS Maps for rural detail, and Kurviger if you want the very curviest routing. Install them, download your offline data, test the setup at home, and you will have navigation covered for anything from a Sunday blast to a two-week tour of the Highlands.
